newsitem.title: UK: Major says N. Irish peace deadlock can be ended.
newsitem.headline: Major says N. Irish peace deadlock can be ended.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major said on Wednesday he was confident that a deadlock in the Northern Irish peace process could be ended but said progress might be slow and painful.

Major, making a traditional Christmas visit to troops and community leaders in the British province, said he was totally committed to the three-year drive to end a decades-old conflict in which thousands of Protestants and Catholics have died.

"We have now hit a hurdle but I think it is a hurdle we will be able to overcome. We have done so in the past. I have every intention of trying to do so again," he told reporters after visiting a school in the town of Dungannon near Belfast.
"I don't believe people can stand in the way of that progress. It may be slow, it may be painful but progress, I am confident, there will be," he said.
Major's optimism is not shared by many local politicians and security analysts, who are gloomy about the short-term prospects for peace in the war-weary region.
The Irish Republican Army (IRA), fighting British rule in the province, shows no sign of restoring a ceasefire it abandoned last February.
Multi-party talks that have limped along since June are due to adjourn for Christmas next week with politicians saying there is no sign of a breakthrough.

"I hope from where we are that we will be able to move forwards," said Major, on his first visit to Northern Ireland since Irish republican bombers struck at the heart of Britain's military presence here in October.
"There is a pause in the move forward but I don't think this pause will last for good provided everybody who speaks about their will to have peace means what they say."
Britain is adamant that the IRA must declare a truce before its Sinn Fein political arm is allowed to join the peace talks. Sinn Fein says it wants talks without preconditions.
Irish nationalist hopes for a new truce received a setback recently when Major rejected proposals from Catholic moderate leader John Hume aimed at speeding Sinn Fein's access to talks.
And as the wrangles continue, tension is building up.
IRA guerrillas killed a soldier and wounded 30 others in a double car bomb attack at British military headquarters in Lisburn on October 7.
It was the first IRA attack in Northern Ireland for two years and came nine months after the guerrillas went back to a war footing with bombs on mainland Britain.
Recent explosives and armaments finds have fuelled British fears that republican guerrillas are planning further attacks.

Northern Ireland's 60 per cent Protestant majority strongly supports rule from London, but the Catholic minority, some of whom back the IRA and its Sinn Fein political arm, want an all-Ireland state ruled from Dublin.
U.S. President Bill Clinton and Irish Prime Minister John Bruton on Tuesday called on the IRA to proclaim a truce.
